new_statements.quote: Finalmente hay que señalar que el acento de los topónimos con esta terminación es agudo y no concuerda con los anteriormente estudiados con las terminaciones -*mal, -*lap, -*cat y -*oc, ya que todos ellos son graves. Es probable que este segmento toponímico no sea de filiación chacha, sino de otra lengua, quizás del quechua [...]
new_statements.translation: Finally it must be pointed out that the stress of the toponyms with this ending [-ran] is oxytone (final) and does not agree with those studied earlier with the endings -*mal, -*lap, -*cat and -*oc, since all of those are paroxytone (penultimate). It is likely that this toponymic segment is not of Chacha affiliation but of another language, perhaps Quechua [...]

new_statements.rule_in_words: The place names Valqui accepts as Chacha (endings -mal, -lap, -cat/-gat, -oc) are all pronounced with penultimate stress, and the author uses this as a diagnostic: names in -ran, which carry final stress, are judged non-Chacha. Because these names are a monosyllabic root plus a monosyllabic ending, penultimate stress coincides with root-initial stress; in his own corpus (PDF p. 62) forms with a paragogic -e are transcribed with stress on the root, i.e. antepenultimate ([kúlape], [tólape], [ó ape], [sí gaèe], [pé gote]), so the underlying pattern is stress on the (first) root syllable rather than a strict penult count.
new_statements.exceptions: The -ran toponyms (Laurán, Llorán, Terán, Quimbalerán, Sipañerán) are oxytone and are therefore attributed to another language; the corpus also transcribes the -mal toponym Osmal as [osmál] with final stress (PDF pp. 62, 65) without comment, contradicting the 'todos ellos son graves' generalisation.
new_statements.domain_note: Not a description of Chacha word stress: Chacha is extinct and unattested; the statement concerns the present-day pronunciation (by Quechua and Spanish speakers of La Jalca Grande) of place names reconstructed as Chacha. Domain = isolated citation forms of toponyms. The related Chachapoyas Quechua first-syllable stress (Taylor 1996/2000, Valqui 2018/2020) was once attributed to a Chacha substrate, a claim now disputed by Valqui himself.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the Chacha (chachapuya) toponymic residue of the district of La Jalca Grande (Chachapoyas province, Amazonas), i.e. chac1253 itself; no dialects are distinguished. The first-syllable stress discussed in Valqui 2018/2020 belongs to Chachapoyas Quechua (Glottolog chac1250), not to Chacha.

sources.note: Only first-hand stress remark for Chacha. Section 5.4 (PDF p. 84): toponyms in -ran are oxytone ('agudo') and 'no concuerda con los anteriormente estudiados con las terminaciones -*mal, -*lap, -*cat y -*oc, ya que todos ellos son graves' (paroxytone). Corpus table 4.4 (PDF p. 62) transcribes the Chacha-origin toponyms with stress on the root/first syllable: [gómal], [yúmal], [èímal], [swímal], [kúlape], [tólape]~[tólap], [ó ape], [sí gaèe], [tó gaèe], [pé gote], but [osmál] final. Sections 5.2.3 and 6.1.1 (reconstructed phonology) list vowels/consonants only and say nothing about accent. Also…

sources.citation: Valqui Culqui, Jairo. 2020. Patrones acentuales en el quechua de Chachapoyas y su implicancia para la reconstrucción del protoquechua. Tesis doctoral, UNMSM, Lima. 208 pp. hdl:20.500.12672/11681
sources.note: Acoustic and phonological study of Chachapoyas Quechua stress (main stress on the first syllable); mentions the Chacha substrate hypothesis (Taylor 2000) only to reject it in favour of Proto-Quechua inheritance. Nothing on Chacha word stress.
No references at all listed; classification 'Unclassifiable', AES extinct.

sources.citation: Ziemendorff, M., J. H. Rodríguez Villa, S. Ziemendorff & J. Valqui Culqui. 2024. La revisita al repartimiento de Yapa en 1617: la primera evidencia de la vigencia de un idioma propio del área Chachapoyas en el siglo XVII. Chungará (Arica) 56(1): 159-179.
sources.note: Ethnohistorical: first documentary mention (1617) of a local non-Quechua language; analyses anthroponyms as monosyllabic elements (Taylor 2000: 14). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Valqui Culqui, J., M. Ziemendorff, S. Ziemendorff & G. Oisel. 2023. Consideraciones histórico-lingüísticas acerca del topónimo Kuélap. INDIANA 40(1): 131-154.
sources.note: Etymology of Kuélap; segments -lap toponyms into monosyllabic root + -lap (Kuélap, Yálape, Óllape, Tálape, Conila) with paragogic -e; accents written on the root syllable but no explicit statement about stress.

sources.citation: Ziemendorff, M., J. Valqui Culqui & S. Ziemendorff. 2023. Observaciones metodológicas sobre el estudio de lenguas extintas en el nororiente peruano: el caso del chacha. Letras (Lima) 94(139): 16-32. doi:10.30920/letras.94.139.2
sources.note: States that first-syllable accentuation of Amazonas Quechua 'era atribuido a un sustrato chacha; empero, ahora se torna discutible' (Valqui 2018, 2020) and that the only characteristic given as certain about Chacha is its monosyllabic tendency (p. 22 region). No direct statement about Chacha stress.

sources.citation: Rojas-Berscia, Luis Miguel. 2020. The Chachapuya language and Proto-Kawapanan: lexical affinities and hypothetical contact scenarios. INDIANA 37(1): 155-188. doi:10.18441/ind.v37i1.155-188
sources.note: Reproduces Taylor's (2000: 16, 18) syllable canon and consonant chart for Chachapuya (pp. 159-160); argues the apparent monosyllabicity results from vowel reduction (p. 171). No mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Valqui, Jairo. 2018. El acento en el quechua de Chachapoyas: un sustrato de la lengua chacha o un vestigio protoquechua. Letras (Lima) 89(130): 79-99. doi:10.30920/letras.89.130.4
sources.note: About Chachapoyas QUECHUA stress (first-syllable main stress in nouns and verbs, Cuadro 2 p. 96), not Chacha. Reports Taylor (2000: 37-38) thought the first-syllable stress of Chachapoyas Quechua could be a substrate from the old Chachapoya language; Valqui argues instead it is a Proto-Quechua vestige (p. 97). No statement about Chacha stress itself.

sources.citation: Valqui, Jairo & Michaela Ziemendorff. 2016. Vestigios de una lengua originaria en el territorio de la cultura chachapoya. Letras (Lima) 87(125): 5-32. doi:10.30920/letras.87.125.1
sources.note: Silent on stress. Gives syllable canon of anthroponyms (VC, CV, CVC, CGV, CVG, CGVC, CVGC) and the monosyllabic-root tendency (p. 28); toponyms cited with Spanish orthographic accents (Cuémal, Shíngache, Tóngate) but no statement about accent.
Tertiary; phonology notes (five vowels, voiced initial stops, palatalisation) drawn from Adelaar & Muysken 2004: 406-407 and Valqui; no stress statement. Used only to assemble the bibliography.
